explanations.answer: Their eyes don't see and their ears don't hear
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. The LORD says they “…have eyes but do not see…” and “…have ears but do not hear.” (Jeremiah 5:21). The equipment is all there and they still don't see or hear. It's like a phone buzzing in your jacket all afternoon and you never notice.

explanations.answer: They see and hear but forget it all fast
explanations.explanation: Close, friend, but forgetting isn't what the LORD says here. He says they “…have eyes but do not see…” and “…have ears but do not hear.” (Jeremiah 5:21). The problem is that they don't see or hear, not that they forget.

explanations.answer: They see and hear but never speak up
explanations.explanation: Speaking up doesn't come into it, friend. The LORD puts the problem right at the eyes and ears: they “…have eyes but do not see…” and “…have ears but do not hear.” (Jeremiah 5:21). Their mouths aren't the issue in this verse. It's the taking in that isn't happening.

Yes, the sand. The LORD says He “…set the sand as the boundary for the sea, an enduring barrier it cannot cross?” (Jeremiah 5:22). Think about that for a second. The whole sea held back by something you can pour out of your shoe.

Good guess, but the LORD doesn't name a river here. He says He set the sand as the boundary for the sea (Jeremiah 5:22). A river runs into a sea, so it wouldn't make much of a fence. The verse is all about sand.

A mountain would be a big fence, friend, but that's not what the LORD names. He says He set the sand as the boundary for the sea (Jeremiah 5:22). I think the sand is the surprising part. It's a tiny thing holding back a huge thing.

The first half is right, but the second half doesn't hold. The LORD says the waves surge and roar, yet “…they cannot prevail.” and “…cannot cross it.” (Jeremiah 5:22). So the waves never break through. They just keep making a lot of noise.

That's right, baker. The LORD says “The waves surge, but they cannot prevail. They roar but cannot cross it.” (Jeremiah 5:22). The waves put on a big show and the boundary doesn't budge. The sea stays where He put it every time.

Right on. The LORD says “…these people have stubborn and rebellious hearts.” (Jeremiah 5:23). Right before it, He talks about the sea and the sand boundary He set for it (Jeremiah 5:22). Then He turns to His people's hearts.

That's not what the LORD says, friend. He actually asks them, “Do you not fear Me?” (Jeremiah 5:22). Then He says their hearts are stubborn and rebellious (Jeremiah 5:23). Tired and afraid doesn't match either one.

The sorry part isn't in the verse, friend. The LORD says their hearts are stubborn and rebellious, and that “They have turned aside and gone away.” (Jeremiah 5:23). Nothing there about being sorry. I think that's what makes the words so heavy.

That's the one. The LORD “…gives the rains, both autumn and spring, in season…” (Jeremiah 5:24). The same verse says He keeps the appointed weeks of harvest. Rains and harvest weeks, both named in one verse.

Winds are real weather, friend, but they aren't what the verse names. It says the LORD “…gives the rains, both autumn and spring, in season…” (Jeremiah 5:24). Rain is what feeds a harvest, so it fits right alongside the appointed weeks.
Frost won't do it, friend. The verse says the LORD “…gives the rains, both autumn and spring, in season…” (Jeremiah 5:24). Frost isn't in that verse at all. I'd keep the frost out of this batch.

True, baker. The LORD says “Your iniquities have diverted these from you; your sins have deprived you of My bounty.” (Jeremiah 5:25). The gifts were His and the diverting came from their sins. It's heavy to read, and He says it plainly.

That's not what the verse says, friend. The LORD says “Your iniquities have diverted these from you; your sins have deprived you of My bounty.” (Jeremiah 5:25). So it's their own iniquities and sins, and it's stated right there. This one is True.
Men, baker. The LORD says these wicked men “…set a trap to catch men.” (Jeremiah 5:26). A fowler hides to catch birds, and these ones hide to catch people. That's a hard line to read.

Lambs aren't in the verse, friend. The LORD says these wicked men “…set a trap to catch men.” (Jeremiah 5:26). A bird catcher's trap is the picture, but people are the catch. I think that's what makes it sting.

Not foxes, friend. The LORD says these wicked men “…set a trap to catch men.” (Jeremiah 5:26). They watch like fowlers, but the ones they're after are people. That's the part that should make you sit up.

Deceit, that's it. The LORD says “Like cages full of birds, so their houses are full of deceit.” (Jeremiah 5:27). A cage full of birds is hard to miss. These houses are just as packed, only with deceit.

Laughter would be a lovely thing to fill a house with, friend, but that's not the verse. The LORD says their houses are full of deceit (Jeremiah 5:27). The picture is a cage packed with birds, and these houses are just as packed, with deceit.

Sorrow isn't what the verse says, friend. The LORD says “Like cages full of birds, so their houses are full of deceit.” (Jeremiah 5:27). These houses are packed, but with deceit. Nothing in the text says these men feel sorrow.
It goes the other way, friend. The LORD says “Therefore they have become powerful and rich.” (Jeremiah 5:27). The deceit hasn't left them poor or weak at all. That's the unsettling part.
Right, baker. The LORD says “Therefore they have become powerful and rich.” (Jeremiah 5:27). Their deceit got them ahead instead of dragging them down. The verse says so plainly.

Yes, the fatherless. The LORD says “They have not taken up the cause of the fatherless, that they might prosper…” (Jeremiah 5:28). These men had plenty and still didn't do it. Next to it He says they haven't defended the rights of the needy.

Soldiers aren't named here, friend. The LORD says these men have “…not taken up the cause of the fatherless…” (Jeremiah 5:28). They also haven't defended the rights of the needy. Those are the two the verse names.

Not the merchants, friend. The verse says they have “…not taken up the cause of the fatherless…” (Jeremiah 5:28). Right after that, the needy come up too. Those are the people who didn't get defended.
That's right, baker. The passage says “The prophets prophesy falsely…” (Jeremiah 5:31). I think that's a heavy line to read.
They're anything but silent, friend. The passage says “The prophets prophesy falsely…” (Jeremiah 5:31). The trouble is what they're saying, not that they've stopped talking.
Leaving the land isn't in the verse, friend. The passage says “The prophets prophesy falsely…” (Jeremiah 5:31). That's what they're doing. Prophesying falsely is the thing the verse names.
Their own, baker. The passage says “…the priests rule by their own authority.” (Jeremiah 5:31). The LORD's and the king's aren't named there. Their own is the one the verse gives.
That's the opposite, friend. The passage says “…the priests rule by their own authority.” (Jeremiah 5:31). It's their own and not the LORD's. That's why it's in the list of shocking things.

The king isn't mentioned here, friend. The passage says “…the priests rule by their own authority.” (Jeremiah 5:31). It's their own authority they're ruling by. That's a short verse with a lot packed in.

True, baker. The passage says “My people love it so…” (Jeremiah 5:31). That comes right after the prophets prophesying falsely and the priests ruling by their own authority. That's what makes the closing question hit so hard.
That's not what it says, friend. The LORD says “My people love it so, but what will you do in the end?” (Jeremiah 5:31). They don't just put up with it. They love it, so this one is True.
